questions.text: What distinguishes signing-key rotation from JWKS refresh in this lesson?

options.A: The resource server rotates private keys; the authorization server refreshes its token cache.
options.B: Both actions mint a new signing key whenever a token has an unknown kid.
options.C: Rotation changes issuer keys; refresh fetches the published key set into the resource server’s cache.
options.D: Refresh extends token expiry; rotation changes the token’s intended audience.

questions.explanation: The authorization server creates and retires signing keys. The resource server fetches their published set for verification; it does not create issuer keys.

questions.text: An opaque-token introspection service is unavailable during a protected tool call. Which behavior matches the lesson’s declared failure policy?

options.A: Fail closed and report the dependency failure without executing the tool.
options.B: Treat the token as active if its string has the expected prefix.
options.C: Decode the opaque token locally and trust any recovered fields.
options.D: Skip authorization temporarily and record the outage afterward.

questions.explanation: Introspection failure cannot establish active status or authorization. Protected calls must fail closed rather than turn network failure into access.

questions.text: ResourceServer.validate decodes a well-formed token whose iss is not in allowed_issuers. According to the supplied code, what happens before any JWKS lookup?

options.A: It refreshes JWKS for the token-supplied issuer and then checks trust.
options.B: It accepts the issuer if the audience matches this resource.
options.C: It selects a trusted issuer with the same key ID and verifies there.
options.D: It returns valid=False with HTTP401 and "iss not allowed" without refreshing JWKS.

questions.explanation: The issuer allowlist check runs before cache lookup or refresh, so an untrusted issuer is refused without a key fetch.
